### Why some AI tools waste money
URL: https://purcellventures.co/blog/why-most-ai-tools-waste-money

Many small business AI tools fail because the workflow they attach to was already broken. Three questions to check yours before you buy.

**The question to ask before any AI purchase** Before you buy an AI tool, answer this: if I had a human assistant doing this exact task for free, would my business improve?

**What AI does well** AI mostly does two things well: generating drafts (writing, summaries, structured outputs) and pattern matching at scale (categorizing, ranking, surfacing). In both cases it produces a first version that a person then finishes.

When I set them up, I connect each one to where its output goes. The chatbot connects to your booking system, the content generator publishes to your blog, and the FAQ builder writes to your live site.

### 121 businesses near the University of Alabama, audited
URL: https://purcellventures.co/blog/121-businesses-near-campus

An audit of every independent business within 2500 metres of the Quad, and how many of them list a website a machine can reach.

**What I measured** The source is the OpenStreetMap website tag , which volunteers maintain, and a business with no website recorded there might still have one. The data cannot show whether ninety-four businesses near campus have a website.

**By category** Restaurants do best, and they still clear only one in four. Every laundry, florist, jeweller, tailor, ice cream shop, phone repair place and car repair shop in the circle came back with nothing.

**The number that surprised me** Twenty-three of the 121 have opening hours recorded anywhere a machine can read them.

**Where a website does not help** I build websites, so you could read this as a pitch for my own service. Two things cut against that reading.

**What happens next** I am visiting these places and writing about them one at a time. For each one I write who runs it, how long it has been here, what it does well, and what a student trying to find it runs into. The series is called the Storefront Project . I feature businesses whether or not they are clients.

**Method** I ran one Overpass query against OpenStreetMap for shops and food businesses within 2500 metres of the Quad, on 20 August 2026. I dropped anything tagged with a chain brand. I sent an HTTP request to every listed website and counted a 403 or a 405 as working, because plenty of live sites refuse a bare HEAD. The script is scout.py and re-running it reproduces every figure above.

### Every post on my blog was telling Google not to index it
URL: https://purcellventures.co/blog/canonical-tag-noindex

One line in a Next.js layout pointed nine blog posts' canonical tags at the index page, telling Google to skip them. How to check your site and fix it.

**What that tells a search engine** A canonical tag tells a search engine that this page and the target page are the same content, and that the target is the one to keep. Google treats it as a strong signal. Google's documentation on consolidating duplicate URLs describes this consolidation behaviour.

**The fix that failed and the fix that worked** The obvious fix is to move the canonical from the layout onto the index page itself. That failed for me: app/blog/page.tsx is a client component, and client components cannot export metadata. That is probably how it ended up in the layout to begin with.

**Testing for this kind of bug** This is the third bug of this kind I have hit this year. In each one, a setting made once and inherited widely failed without an error.

### Five security holes I keep finding in small production apps
URL: https://purcellventures.co/blog/small-app-security-checklist

Security holes from seven read-only audits of small production apps: open row-level security, paid API routes with no auth, forgeable cookies and more.

**Row-level security is on and enforcing nothing** This was the most common one in my audits, and it is easy to miss because the dashboard shows green.

**Paid API routes with no authentication** Small apps often have server routes that call a metered service, such as a language model or a maps API. Developers skip authentication on these routes because during development they are the only ones who know the URL. That URL is in your JavaScript bundle, where anyone can read it.

**An auth cookie anyone can set** This one starts when a developer writes a placeholder login check during the build and never replaces it. The app sets a cookie on login, and the check asks whether the cookie exists, or whether it equals a known constant.

**Sequential identifiers as authorisation** Say a record is at /thing/41 and a logged-in user requests /thing/42 . Many small apps never check whether that user may see it.

**Input that becomes markup** This is text a user typed, such as a display name or a review, rendered back out as HTML. Injection is on the OWASP Top Ten , and I still found it.

**How I run one of these audits** I keep every audit read-only. The output is a list, and the fixes happen later in a planned session.

**Why the developer misses these** Each of these problems sits in code that works. The developer tested that the features work, and that testing does not show what an attacker could do.

URL: https://purcellventures.co/blog/is-your-business-invisible

Seven checks a small business owner can run in ten minutes, with no tools or account, to see what a customer with a phone finds. Based on 121 local businesses.

**Starting with a phone that is not yours** Borrow one, or open a private window and sign out of everything. Your own phone has visited your website and remembers your searches, so it shows you results a new customer will not see. Every check below depends on starting clean.

**The seven checks** Add the town to the name: "Joe's Barbers Tuscaloosa." Look at the first result. If it is a directory site you have never logged into, a Facebook page you stopped updating, or a competitor, you have your answer, and fixing that comes before the other checks.

**When you do not need a website** I build websites, so read this with that in mind.

**If you are near campus** I am writing about independent businesses around the University of Alabama, one at a time. Each post covers who runs the business, how long it has been there, what it does well and what a student trying to find it runs into. The series is the Storefront Project , and being featured is free.

**Questions** The most common reason is that nobody has claimed the Google Business Profile. Google may have created a listing without you, in which case you claim it instead of creating a new one. Creating a second listing for a business that already has one produces a duplicate, and Google can hide duplicates.

Services University of Alabama students already pay for in tuition and fees: University Recreation, the Writing Center, the Career Center, CrimsonRide and more.

### Five failures from running fifteen AI agents
URL: https://purcellventures.co/blog/what-the-agents-get-wrong

Five failures from running fifteen AI agents in production, including a gate that always passed, eleven agents never called and findings that closed themselves.

**A gate that always passed** The deal pipeline moves work between agents and stops at gates that need a human. One of those gates asked me whether a client had responded to a proposal.

**Twenty proposals with the internal notes still in them** The proposal agent drafted 20 documents. Every one carried internal markers: reasoning meant for me, confidence hedges, and notes about the client written for the person deciding whether to send.

**Eleven of the fifteen were never being called** For weeks the daily run reported success while eleven of the fifteen agents were never called. Those eleven existed and had been tested, but because the script exited zero, the morning report said every agent ran.

**Findings that closed themselves** The audit agent records findings and closes them when the underlying problem is gone. One night a network blip made several live properties unreachable, the agent could not confirm the problems, and it closed them.

**An agent with access nobody granted** Each agent runs a model inside a wrapper that reads context, reasons, validates and writes. Its prompt described the scope of what it should touch.

**What has worked** The auditing agents cannot change anything. Separating the agents that find problems from the agents that fix them took one design decision.

### New College at Alabama, explained by someone in it
URL: https://purcellventures.co/blog/new-college-alabama

How New College at the University of Alabama works: the self-designed degree, the depth study, the seminars, the Levitetz program, and the case for and against.

**What it is** New College is an interdisciplinary program inside the Barefield College of Arts and Sciences at the University of Alabama. It started in 1971.

**Terms you will hear in the first week** A depth study is your self-designed concentration. Existing examples include Socio-Legal Studies, Psycho-Social Sciences and Neuroscience. Mine combines psychology and data science, aimed at psychiatry and at how AI can reduce the administrative load on mental health clinicians.

**Reasons to choose it** If your question does not fit one department, a traditional major makes you pick the closest one and spend four years taking courses next to the subject you wanted to study.

**Reasons against it** Few people outside the program know what it is. A graduate admissions committee or a recruiter understands "psychology" right away. "A self-designed depth study in psycho-social sciences" needs a sentence of explanation every time, and you will explain it often.

**Who should pick it** Pick it if you can already say, in one sentence, the question your degree is for.

**Practical details** New College is reachable at (205) 348-4600 or ncfrndsk@ua.edu. It combines with the Honors College, which is what I am doing. Ask about the depth study proposal process early, because it shapes which courses are worth taking in your first year instead of your third.

### How to audit every business in your town in an afternoon
URL: https://purcellventures.co/blog/audit-every-business-in-your-town

How to audit every business in your town in an afternoon: one free Overpass query on OpenStreetMap, one HTTP request per site, and two common mistakes.

**The data source** OpenStreetMap, queried through Overpass . Volunteers maintain it, it is openly licensed, it permits this use, and it carries exactly the tag that matters: website .

**Filtering to independents** You do not want chains. Do not try to detect them by name, because you will build a list of brand strings and it will be wrong in both directions.

**Checking each website** For each business with a website tag, make a request and see what happens. Both of my mistakes happened at this step.

**Mistake one: relying on HEAD requests** I sent HEAD requests, because they are cheap and you only need the status code.

**Mistake two: claiming more than the data shows** The headline I wanted was "93 businesses near campus have no website." The data does not support it.

**What to do with the result** Sort the businesses that list a website which no longer answers to the top, because they already decided a site was worth paying for and theirs broke. That is a much shorter conversation than convincing somebody they need one.

**What I am using it for** My script is under two hundred lines. I am using it to write about independent businesses near campus , one at a time. If you run it on your town and find something surprising, I would like to hear it .

### What registering an LLC at seventeen involved
URL: https://purcellventures.co/blog/llc-at-seventeen

Registering an LLC at seventeen: the Georgia filing, the EIN, the bank account, the registered agent question and a rename nine months later. Not legal advice.

**The filing itself is the easy part** The filing is an online form with a name, an address, a registered agent and a fee. Choosing the name took me longer than filing it. You get a control number and a public record, and at that point the company exists.

**The registered agent and the public address** Somebody has to be the legal point of contact, and for a one-person company that is usually you. That address goes on a public filing.

**The EIN takes ten minutes and is free** You get it directly from the IRS . Some sites charge for an EIN even though the IRS issues it free, so skip any page that asks for money.

**The bank account is the hardest part** Banks have their own policies about account holders under eighteen, and those policies are separate from state law about whether a minor can form an LLC. Branch policies varied, and one branch told me yes on the phone and no at the desk.

**Renaming the company** I filed as Zultar LLC and amended the name to Purcell Ventures LLC on 27 January 2026. The entity, the control number and the EIN stayed the same.

**What the LLC does and does not do for you** It gives you a legal entity that can hold a bank account, sign a contract, and invoice a client. For most small operations that is most of the value.

**The sequence I followed** I would stress that last step most to anybody doing this young, because it is easy to spend months on paperwork before sending a single invoice.

### The cold email that got me a client, and the ones that did not
URL: https://purcellventures.co/blog/cold-outreach-that-worked

The cold email that got me a client: lead with a specific observation, send a built page instead of describing one, and three sentences to cut.

**The email most people send first** I wrote this one first, like most people do.

**Opening with something you noticed** The version that works opens with something specific and checkable about their business. Write an observation about it, and skip the praise.

**Building the page first, then sending it** The best thing I did in cold outreach was build first and send the link: a live page at its own URL that loads on their phone, with a note asking whether they want it.

**Three sentences to cut** "I hope this email finds you well." It tells the reader the next paragraph is a template.

**My age** I was seventeen when I started sending these, and my first instinct was to hide it. That would have backfired, because it comes out eventually, and when it comes out after a client has decided to trust you, it looks like concealment.

**Follow-up** Send one message about a week later that adds something new. Most of my replies came on the second contact and almost none came on the third, so a third contact is rarely worth sending.

### Claiming your own Google listing: a twenty-minute job
URL: https://purcellventures.co/blog/claim-your-google-listing

How to claim and fill out a Google Business Profile yourself in twenty minutes: every field, hiding a home address, and what gets a listing suspended.

**What a Google Business Profile is** A Google Business Profile is the panel that appears beside search results with your name, hours, phone, photos, reviews and a map. It is also what puts you in the map section at the top of a "near me" search.

**Step by step** Search your business name on Google first. If a panel appears, look for "Own this business?" or "Claim this business" and start there. Creating a second profile for a business that already has one is the most common way people end up with a duplicate, and Google may suppress duplicates.

**Reviews** A listing with recent reviews gives a searcher more to go on than one with none.

**A five-minute monthly check** The monthly check is also how you would find out that someone marked you permanently closed.

**When to get help** Most owners can do all of this without help. Help is worth paying for when you have a duplicate listing you cannot merge, a suspension you do not understand, or several locations. If you are near the University of Alabama and stuck on one of those, ask me and I will tell you what I would do: elijah@purcellventures.co .

**Questions** It depends on the method. Postcard verification takes up to two weeks. Phone, email and video verification are faster. Video means recording a short walkthrough showing your signage, your equipment and your address, so have those visible before you start. Do not create a second listing while you are waiting for a postcard.

### Auditing your own site the way a crawler does, with curl
URL: https://purcellventures.co/blog/audit-your-site-like-a-crawler

Nine checks to run on your live site with curl and no account: wrong canonical tags, duplicate titles, sitemap and robots conflicts, missing structured data.

**1. Pages that canonicalise to a different URL** This check found the problem that kept nine of my pages out of Google. A canonical tag pointing somewhere else says "I am a duplicate, index that instead," and Google does exactly that.

**2. Pages set to noindex by accident** curl -sIL https://example.com/page | grep -i x-robots-tag curl -sL https://example.com/page | grep -o '<meta name="robots"[^>]*' Check the header as well as the tag. An X-Robots-Tag set at the edge or in middleware is invisible in the HTML and overrides everything you can see in the source, and Google treats the two as equivalent directives .

**3. Sitemap URLs that robots.txt blocks** A URL that appears in the sitemap and is also disallowed in robots.txt is a contradiction. The page can still show up in results as a bare link with no description, because the crawler was never allowed to read it. The sitemap documentation says a sitemap asks for a crawl and does not override robots.txt.

**4. Duplicate page titles** Duplicate titles waste crawl budget and make a search engine choose between your own pages. Mine came from three section layouts handing their title to every child.

**5. Structured data that fails to parse** Markup that exists can still be broken, so test that it parses. Google skips a JSON-LD block with a trailing comma without any warning, and the page behaves as if you never wrote it. Valid markup does not replace the content itself, so also read Google's guidance on which content it evaluates .

**6. One @id for each person or organisation** If your site names a person or an organisation in several places, every one of those nodes needs the same @id . Without it you are describing several different people who happen to share a name, on your own domain, which is the ambiguity the markup exists to remove.

**7. The search term in the page title** The title tag is a strong on-page signal for a query, and my homepage did not contain my own name, which meant the highest-authority page on my domain could not rank for it.

**8. Page speed** curl -sL -o /dev/null -w 'ttfb %{time_starttransfer}s total %{time_total}s %{size_download} bytes\n' \ https://example.com/page Time to first byte is the number worth watching, because it is the part your hosting and your server code control. If it is under 200 milliseconds, speed is not your bottleneck and your time is better spent on the other checks.

### What one operator can deliver
URL: https://purcellventures.co/blog/what-one-operator-can-deliver

How much work a one-person software company can carry, what happens when two clients want the same fortnight, and three signs you are being oversold.

**Measuring capacity in builds** I count capacity in builds, because hours miss how a build works. A build is a sequence with waiting in it: you scope, you build, you send it, you wait for feedback, you revise, you launch. The waiting breaks up everything around it, so it does not turn into free time.

**What happens when two clients want the same fortnight** The second client waits, so the question to ask a solo operator is how they decide who goes second.

**What an agency does better** Continuity is the first. If I became unavailable, your site would be a repository and a hosting account with nobody who knows why anything is the way it is, while an agency has other people. To protect yourself, get admin access to everything, in your own name, from day one. If a provider resists that, leave.

**What a solo operator does better** The person you talked to is the person who builds it. Nothing is lost between the conversation and the work, because there is no handoff.

**Three signs you are being oversold** The first is an offer of unlimited anything. Unlimited revisions from a one-person shop means either a cap that will appear later or a person who is about to resent your project.

**How to decide** Ask three questions and listen to whether the answers are specific.

### What a small business website costs
URL: https://purcellventures.co/blog/what-a-website-actually-costs

What a small business website costs: why one site gets quotes from $400 to $15,000, what a monthly plan includes, and the ongoing costs that quotes leave out.

**What the price pays for** The first is design, which means deciding what the site looks like. It ranges from picking a template to creating a visual identity, and it drives much of the spread.

**The costs quotes leave out** These costs continue after you pay the invoice, whether or not the quote mentions them.

**How to judge whether a quote is fair** A $10,000 site can be good value and a $500 site can be a waste. Judge a quote by what it includes.

**What a customer is worth to you** Work out what one customer is worth, and how many extra customers would make the site pay for itself.

### What psychology has to do with the software I build
URL: https://purcellventures.co/blog/psychology-and-software

Within-subject design, base rates and construct validity: three ideas from a first-semester psychology methods course that changed software I had shipped.

**Within-subject design** The rule, as the APA defines it , is that you measure a person against their own baseline rather than against everybody else's. My product did the opposite.

**Base rates** The second idea that transferred is base rates. A test that is ninety-nine per cent accurate for a condition affecting one person in ten thousand produces far more false positives than true ones, and most people's intuition says otherwise.

**Construct validity** Psychology spends a lot of effort on whether the thing you measured is the thing you meant. Construct validity asks whether a measurement is of the right thing, however precise it is.

**Why I am studying both** The plan is psychiatry, and the specific thing I want to work on is how much administrative load a clinician carries that could be carried by something else, starting with notes and documentation.

### My team page lists fifteen people who do not exist
URL: https://purcellventures.co/blog/ai-team-page-honesty

Why a company running AI agents should name them, say they are software in the first sentence, and never let one sign an email as a human. The rules I enforce.

**Why the agents have names** The alternative is describing them as a system, which tells a client little. "Automated proposal generation" says nothing about what happens on a Tuesday. "Quentin drafts the proposal, Cecily checks it for anything internal, and it does not leave the building until both have passed it" tells you exactly what happens, and the names make the order easy to follow.

**Why the first sentence has to say what they are** First, clients find out. If the page showed invented colleagues with stock photographs, a client would eventually ask to speak to Margot, and I would have to admit she does not exist.

**What this costs** It costs me some credibility. "One person and fifteen scripts" sounds smaller than "our team," and some prospects would have been more impressed by the second phrase.

**If you are building something similar** Say what it is on the page where you say what it does. Put the disclosure inside the function that sends. If you would be uncomfortable having a client read a sentence about your company back to you, rewrite it.

### Can an AI find your business? A test you can run in five minutes
URL: https://purcellventures.co/blog/can-ai-find-your-business

Can an AI find your business? A five-minute test shows what ChatGPT and Google's AI answer say about you, why they get it wrong, and four fixes that help.

**The five-minute test** Run it signed out, in a private window, on a device that has not been to your website.

**Why they get it wrong** They read cached copies. A correction to your website can take weeks to show up in the answer.

**Four fixes** 1. Say the plain sentence somewhere on your site. "Joe's Barbers is a barber shop on 15th Street in Tuscaloosa, Alabama, open Tuesday to Saturday." That is the sentence an assistant will use, and if it does not exist on your site it will use one from somewhere you do not control.

**What does not work** Keyword stuffing does not work, and neither does paying for an "AI optimisation" service that will not tell you what it does, or adding a page of text written for machines. Assistants summarise pages, and a page that reads as machine-written produces a poor summary.

**Why the Google Business Profile comes first** Assistant answers about local businesses draw on listings like Google Business Profile and directories, and the Google listing is free. Claim your Google Business Profile and put accurate hours in it before you think about any of this.

**Questions** Most of the work is the same work as being findable in the first place: a claimed listing, consistent details across sources, and pages that plainly state facts. Before paying anyone for AI optimisation, ask them to list exactly what they will change. If they will not, do not hire them.

### How to write a page an AI will quote
URL: https://purcellventures.co/blog/write-a-page-an-ai-will-quote

Answer engine optimisation in plain terms: the sentence shape a model can lift, what FAQPage schema still does, what llms.txt is for, and why indexing is first.

**How the two jobs differ** A search engine ranks pages, while an answer engine extracts sentences . A page built to rank well can still give an answer engine nothing it can quote.

**Sentences that make sense on their own** The test: cut any sentence out of your page, show it to someone who has not read the rest, and see whether it still means anything.

**Third person for facts about a person** A page that says "I am nineteen and I run a software company" cannot be lifted and presented as a fact about a named entity, because a model has no way to attach "I" to anything.

**FAQPage schema** FAQPage is the format that hands a machine a question and a self-contained answer as structured data.

**One ID for each person or company** If your site names a person or company in several places, every one of those structured data nodes needs the same @id . Otherwise you are describing several entities that happen to share a name, on your own domain.

**Telling apart people with the same name** If somebody shares your name, say which one you are. schema.org has disambiguatingDescription for exactly this, and the plain-prose version belongs on the page too.

**llms.txt** llms.txt is a plain-text file at the root of your site describing what is on it and where. Adoption is not universal and nobody should promise you results from it.

**Inline source citations** Cite external sources in the text, and link them.

### Building a campus events site from six sources
URL: https://purcellventures.co/blog/six-sources-one-page

How UA Today merges six feeds of University of Alabama events into one page, and why the hard part is catching a source that stops sending events with no error.

**Combining the feeds** Fetching and normalising six feeds took a day of work. The feeds use different date formats, describe locations differently, and disagree on whether a recurring event is one record or forty.

**Detecting a source that stops without an error** A source that returns an error is easy to catch, because you see the error and fix it.

**Floor checks** The fix is to assert a minimum event count. Each source declares how many events it should plausibly produce, and returning fewer is a failure even when the request succeeded.

**Moderation and the unofficial notice** The first is a moderation queue. Anyone can submit an event, and nothing appears until a person reviews it. For a site with a university's name near it, the cost of one bad listing is much higher than the cost of a slower pipeline.

**What I would do differently** I would write the floor checks first. I added them only after a source went quiet, and until then I was trusting a status report I had never tested.

### What you should own at the end of a website project
URL: https://purcellventures.co/blog/what-you-should-own

The seven accounts and assets that should be in your name when a website project ends, why the domain matters most, and two questions to ask before you sign.

**Why the domain comes first** You can replace everything else with some effort. Code can be rebuilt, hosting can move in a day, and you can recover from losing analytics history.

**Two questions before you sign** "When we finish, which of these will be in my name?" Ask it about the list above, specifically, and get the answer in writing. The answer should be all of them.

**What a provider can reasonably keep** Providers can reasonably keep their own internal tooling, their project management system, and any general-purpose components they built before you and will use again after you. Reusing components is normal, and it keeps prices down.

**If you are already in this situation** Ask for the transfer plainly. Most providers will do it, and some never realised the client wanted it.

### Starting a business as a University of Alabama student
URL: https://purcellventures.co/blog/starting-a-business-at-alabama

Starting a business as a University of Alabama student: the campus resources that apply, why your first customer should be local, and three costly mistakes.

**Local businesses as customers** Campus is a walkable market of thirty-eight thousand people with predictable needs. Several hundred local businesses serve them, and their owners can say yes without a purchasing department.

**Campus resources that help** Most "resources for student entrepreneurs" lists are competitions, and a competition does not bring you customers. These campus services help with running the business.

URL: https://purcellventures.co/courses/ai-automation

How to build automations for your own work: what to automate first, what to leave alone, and how to tell which is which.

**The tools you build** You write each tool yourself, run it on your own machine and keep the code.
